purpose: Mechanical conformance evidence for the structural path walker used by closed-world observed-pair coverage (the `paths(canonical(value))` operator in the generic specification). This is a distinct capability from canonicalIdentityJson conformance (see canonical-identity-json-conformance-v0): the walker enumerates PATHS from a value, it does not serialize a whole value. Freezes what the walker actually does; does not invent semantics. Consumable by any language's test runner without importing production TypeScript -- every vector is plain data.
format_notes: `walk_vectors` each carry a `root` value (or `roots` for a multi-root equal-paths comparison) and `expected_paths`, an object mapping every expected path string to its expected raw leaf value.

`pairwise_vectors` carry `source` and `target` values and assert properties of the observed-pair universe U_obs = paths(canonical(source)) UNION paths(canonical(target)): its path membership and, per path, whether it is present on the source side, the target side, or both.

The string tokens `"$special:undefined"` and `"$special:non_finite"` are placeholder markers wherever a JS-specific value not directly representable in plain JSON is needed (an `undefined` array element, or a non-finite number such as Infinity). A consumer MUST substitute the literal value before use: `$special:undefined` -> the language's absent/undefined-equivalent array-element marker; `$special:non_finite` -> a positive-infinity float. These tokens never appear as intentional string data in any vector below.

IMPORTANT, load-bearing distinction: the walker itself NEVER throws or rejects any value, including a non-finite number or an undefined array element -- it always successfully enumerates paths and preserves the raw leaf value unmodified. Rejection of such values happens strictly downstream, when a SEPARATE comparator call (canonicalIdentityJson) is made on that leaf value -- see canonical-identity-json-conformance-v0's own non_finite/undefined vectors for that separate rejection behavior, and transformation-stability-coverage-failure-semantics-v0.test.ts for how that downstream rejection becomes an `unresolved` evaluation outcome. Vectors here that carry a `$special:*` marker inside `expected_paths` are proving the walker's PERMISSIVE pass-through behavior, not a rejection.

walk_vectors.description: A bare scalar root (not an object) has no field name of its own, so it produces zero observed paths.
Same rule for a string root.
A flat object's own keys become top-level paths.
Nested objects recurse; only the leaf carries a path -- the intermediate key ('a') never appears on its own.
Declaration order of object keys does not affect the resulting path set.
An empty object at the root produces zero observed paths (same result as a bare scalar root).

LOAD-BEARING, non-obvious behavior: a key whose value is an empty object produces ZERO paths for that key -- the key itself never appears in the observed universe, indistinguishable from that key being entirely absent. This is DIFFERENT from an empty array (see empty_array_whole_atom below), which DOES produce a path.
An array is a whole-array leaf atom -- never decomposed into per-index paths.
An empty array IS recorded as a present leaf (contrast empty_object_nested above, which is not).
An array containing nested arrays is captured wholesale at the outer array's path; nothing inside it is further decomposed.
An array nested inside an object still terminates decomposition at the array boundary.
null is a present leaf value, distinct from the key being absent.
false is a present leaf value (not confused with absence).
An empty string is a present leaf value, distinct from the key being absent.

A key explicitly present with an undefined-equivalent value is treated identically to the key being entirely absent -- it produces zero paths, matching the walker's documented undefined-drops-to-absent convention.

The walker does NOT reject an undefined-equivalent element inside an array leaf -- it preserves the raw array, including the special element, unmodified. Rejection (if any) is a separate, downstream comparator concern -- see format_notes.
Same permissive-preservation rule for a non-finite number inside an array leaf.
Recursion depth is unbounded in principle; a 4-level-deep leaf still produces the full dotted path.

pairwise_vectors.description: A path present only on the source side appears in U_obs with source-presence true, target-presence false. Equivalent framing: this is also the present-on-source-to-absent-on-target case.
A path present only on the target side appears in U_obs with source-presence false, target-presence true. Equivalent framing: this is also the absent-on-source-to-present-on-target case.
Control case: a path present on both sides appears once in U_obs with both presence flags true.
A path that never appears on either side is not part of U_obs at all -- confirms the closed-world layering rule: absence on both sides is invisible to this layer, never a coverage mismatch.

mutants.description: Recursively decomposes arrays into per-index paths (e.g. 'tags.0', 'tags.1') instead of treating an array as a whole-array atom.
Silently omits a key whose value is null, instead of recording null as a present leaf.
Unlike the real walker (which produces zero paths for a key mapped to an empty object -- see empty_object_nested), this mutant records an explicit path/leaf for such a key.
Computes the observed-pair universe as source paths only, ignoring any path that exists only on the target side, instead of the union of both sides.
